# Steering Rack Clicking Noise

A clicking noise emanating from the front right tire area of a Mitsubishi Outlander (MY2011, RHD) while steering presents a classic case of driveline or suspension articulation failure. You have already replaced all tie rods, bushes, and the CV boot, yet the sound persists during cornering maneuvers. This specific symptomânoise occurring only when the wheel is turnedâimmediately narrows the diagnostic window to components that physically engage or disengage under lateral load. Since the outer tie rod ends are ruled out, the mechanical load path must be traced back toward the steering rack itself or the inner connection points.

When a vehicle turns, the steering rack converts rotational input from the column into linear extension of the tie rods. If there is play in the rack's internal splines or the mounting bushings, this movement translates directly into an audible click rather than precise wheel rotation. The fact that the suspension was checked implies the control arms and ball joints are likely intact, shifting focus to the rack assembly. A common failure point in this scenario is a worn steering rack pinion shaft or loose rack mount bushings. When the rack mounts are compromised, the entire unit can shift slightly within the chassis frame during sharp turns, causing internal gears to impact their housing or the output shaft to strike the mounting bracket.

Another critical area to investigate is the inner tie rod end where it connects to the rack. Even if the outer ends are new, the inner splines on the rack shaft can wear out independently. This wear creates a gap that collapses under steering load, resulting in a distinct click before the connection tightens up again. To diagnose this without disassembly immediately, try isolating the noise source by lifting the front wheels and manually rocking them while turning the wheel lock-to-lock. If the click is felt through the chassis rather than heard at the wheel end, the issue likely lies within the rack housing or its mounting points.

You might consider a test involving the removal of the inner tie rod from the rack to see if the noise persists when the wheel is turned manually. However, be aware that disconnecting the steering linkage entirely can make the wheel extremely sensitive and dangerous if the vehicle moves while you are under it. A safer approach is to inspect the rack mounting bolts for torque consistency and check for cracks in the rubber bushings using a borescope or by applying UV dye penetrant if available. If the bushings have hardened or cracked, the rack effectively becomes loose relative to the subframe, allowing internal components to rattle against the casing.

Replacing the tie rod ends is often the first line of defense, but it does not address wear inside the rack itself. If the rack output shaft splines are stripped or the internal rack and pinion gear mesh is worn beyond adjustment limits, replacing the entire steering rack assembly may be necessary. This is a significant cost, but attempting to recondition the internal gears often yields unreliable results due to precise tolerances required for safe handling. Always verify that the new rack includes fresh mounting bushings, as installing a refurbished rack onto worn mounts will simply transfer the problem back to the chassis immediately.

If you are looking for a reliable source of parts or technical guidance on steering system repairs, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can sometimes offer insights into aftermarket component quality and sourcing strategies for specific vehicle models. However, the primary focus remains on ensuring the structural integrity of the rack assembly itself. Ignoring a clicking noise that persists after replacing external linkages risks progressive wear that could lead to total steering failure or loss of control under emergency braking or sharp avoidance maneuvers.
